Artwork

A clearer process for approving packaging color

FORME Packaging editorialUpdated October 21, 20263 min read

Screens help communicate direction, while physical references help approve production. Define the paper, printing method and viewing conditions alongside the intended color.

In this guideChoose a physical color referenceReview color on the proposed substrateSeparate artwork approval from color approvalKeep one final production referenceDiscuss your packaging →

Choose a physical color reference

Start with your brand standards and identify the exact reference used for each important color. Record whether a color is intended as a process-color build or a separate spot ink. The same visual goal can require a different approach on coated white card, textured wrap and kraft liner.

Send a physical reference when color is especially important. A photograph of a swatch introduces lighting and camera differences. Keep the reference name, edition or sample identifier in the artwork notes so everyone is discussing the same target.

Review color on the proposed substrate

Paper color and texture influence the printed result. A pale design on a natural kraft surface will not look like the same artwork on a bright white liner. Lamination, varnish and foil add further visual changes. Request a proof that represents the selected material and process as closely as practical.

Large solid areas deserve attention at folds, corners and rubbing surfaces. If the design uses a dark background, check handling marks and the appearance of exposed cut edges. Review these points before approving the final finish.

Separate artwork approval from color approval

  • Confirm content, spelling, logos and barcode placement.
  • Check panel orientation on an assembled mockup.
  • Review overprints, bleeds and process-specific artwork layers.
  • Approve color against an agreed physical reference.
  • Identify any feature the proof cannot reproduce faithfully.

A digital PDF approval can confirm layout without confirming paper feel or a specialist finish. Make the approval scope explicit to avoid treating one file as evidence for every production detail.

Keep one final production reference

Use version numbers for artwork and write down the approved paper and finish. If a material changes, ask whether the color needs another review. Keep the signed sample or proof with the order records and share the same reference with the production team.

For a range using rigid boxes, mailers and white-card cartons, compare the materials together. Coordinated colors may need adjustments across substrates rather than identical ink instructions on every component.
